22.t: Lytell and Signorelli's recording of Sister Kate
22.s: La Rocca says Lytell and Signorelli took his whole Sister Kate arrangement and recorded it, and that his correspondence with Piron predates Clarence Williams coming to New York.
22.q: They took the whole arrangement in total and recorded it. That's what they did. And they made Sister Kate. Now I had correspondence with A.J. Perron. I just can't find it at present. I would like to include that in there to show you that Perron and I correspond before Francis Williams ever came to…

22.t: Copyrighting under his own name and Shields's collaboration
22.s: He explains he put tunes under his own name because bandmates took royalties, and discusses Shields as collaborator.
22.q: Well, I'll tell you why I did that. The reason I did that, because I had so many numbers on my name. And I had to share with the guys in the band. You understand what I mean? I tried to look out for myself. Up to this time, these fellas rode my back. They composed not only with Shields, who…

256.t: Tin Roof Blues: origin, publisher and copyright
256.s: Written as Rusty Rail Blues, retitled by Melrose, with royalties split among many names and a later renewal.
256.ch: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
256.q: So we came up here, Melrose, Waller Melrose, the publisher, which I gave him the title of the house of blues built for his bottom of his music. He's in the real estate business out in Barrington.

10.t: Fickle Fay Creep, Soapsuds and the manuscript Carew found
10.s: Harrison Smith claimed Fickle Fay Creep as another tune; Carew traces it to Soapsuds, recovered through his nephew's records.
10.q: Now, when he did that, Harrison Smith right away claimed that that was a tune by one of his writers, you know. And he said it was the same tune as Just Alone the Echo, which was copyrighted, oh, three, four years before Jelly Roll recorded Fickle Faye Creep. So I went down to the library and I…

83.t: Getting a songwriter a publishing contract
83.s: Matassa explains how his name came to be on a song: the writer had no contract, so he arranged one (Hill and Range, he thinks) and his widow still collects; Wexler is mentioned.
83.q: And so, I said, well, you know, we need to organize all of this stuff and do something. And that's what we did. And I got him a contract with Hill and Range, I think.

619.s: He shows copyrighted songs such as I Got a Woman Doing What You Used to Do and says he never had time to publish or record them.
619.q: Too bad. Just one copy. I got a couple of numbers here now. I got to have recorded. And I got some. I got to record it. My wife took $30,000. $30,000. $50,000. $50,000. $50,000. $50,000. $50,000. And all of that. I had them copyright and everything. And I never did nothing with them yet.

819.t: Tune-writing, band credit and Tiger Rag's origin
819.s: Tunes written collectively by the band, the royalty confusion cleared in 1937-38, and where Tiger Rag came from.
819.q: for a solid week you'll never you'll never get the the mix up on the dixieland that's one of the big mix-ups that happened in years ago you know that was all cleared in 37 and 38 luckily it was all cleared because none of those names everything should have been by the original dixieland there but…

138.t: La Rocca's claimed compositions and joining Laine's band
138.s: Russell asks about tunes La Rocca claimed to write; Laine says he learned them from his band, and repeats the Brunies substitution story.
138.q: He came around, you know, and wanted to come into rehearsal once again and another, and so everything was all right, you know. Then he come out with us, playing jobs, you know, different jobs, and not pay him just as well as I pay the rest of the men.

196.t: Joe Virgis's claimed tunes: Jealous, Jelly Bean, Camel Walk
196.s: Allen says Virgis claimed many tunes; Leclerc confirms Jelly Bean and Camel Walk and who published which of his numbers.
196.q: Yeah, yeah. He wrote Camel Walk. See, I hadn't even remembered that. Camel Walk, yeah. Well, of course, those numbers were published by the Triangle, you see. Now, you see, someday more movies were published by that. Triangle Blues, I think. I think Plessy did that too for me. Yeah. And Cookie. I…

588.t: Writing lyrics to other composers' music
588.s: She wrote lyrics to Guy Warren, Villa-Lobos, Monk and Coltrane tunes, sometimes without permission, which later caused trouble with their families.
588.ch: New York and the Freedom Now years
588.q: Sometimes it's really embarrassing to witness it. They look like a bunch of aborigines. And the men are wearing styles they never even had in Africa. I mean, but this is a prolific strand. It doesn't hang. You have to weight it. Its natural thing is like that. So, we were doing these hair style…

69.t: How many tunes, and what happened to his last five
69.s: He cannot say how many tunes he wrote or list them; the last five or six went to Mills and he has heard nothing since the company was sold.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: Oh, gosh -- quite a bit. It didn't amount to much, but still, they come, and the checks come -- like I said before, they come in amounts of two, three, five dollars. "Lost in Meditation" should have been a good tune, if they only plugged it like they should have. "Perdido" sold a lot with -- who's…

641.t: Inventor claims and Tudie's claim to have written Blues for Jimmy
641.s: Musicians claim to have invented the bowed bass and mute, and Tudie claimed to have written a piece actually from Lucia.
641.ch: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
641.q: See, he claimed he wrote it. And he says, "I want to get extra money for it" -- on this session. And Ory said, "You wrote no such thing." And Bud Scott said, "No, he wrote it." They'd say whatever you said or something.

92.t: Unpaid co-compositions with Dameron and an untitled tune Collins will record
92.s: Dameron took the money from tunes they wrote together such as John's Idea; Collins plans to record an unnamed one himself.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Yes, we did quite a few compositions, you know. Not -- and I never got a penny from any of them, you know, because he would take the money and buy shit with it, you know, this is what he -- that's the expression. And so consequently I would never get in -- I never received a money like John's Idea…

78.t: Tunes lifted by others, and how many songs he composed
78.s: Others sometimes added bars to his melodies and took credit; he estimates 35 or 40 compositions placed with publishers.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Oh, I've listened sometimes to something that sounds quite familiar to me, you know, especially about eight bars of certain things, you know, that you know you thought up, and some guys just put a few more bars with it, you know. They got the credit for the title and all that. Yes, those things…
